A very soft rock composed primarily of the mineral talc. Steatite, commonly called soapstone, is composed of hydrated magnesium silicate.
Soapstone is composed primarily of talc and shares many physical properties with that mineral.
Soapstone is a metamorphic rock that is composed primarily of talc, with varying amounts of chlorite, pyroxenes, micas, amphiboles, carbonates, and other minerals.
Soapstone is relatively soft because of its hi gh talc content, talc having a definitional value of 1 on the Mohs hardness scale.

There is no fixed hardness fo r soapstone because the amount of talc it contains varies widely, from as little as 30% for architectural grades such as those used on countertops, to as much as 80% for carving grades.
Common, non-architectural grades of soapstone can just barely be scratched wi th a fingernail and are thus considered to have a hardness of 2.5 on the Mohs scale.
If a candidate rock cannot be scratched with a knife blade (hardness of 5.5), it is not soapstone.
Native steatite is so soft it can be scratched with a fingernail, but baking results in dehydration and hardening of the stone.
Its name is derived from its "soapy" feel and softness.
Soft er grades may feel soapy when touched, hence the name.
Soapstone with a fine grain size works best for highly detailed carvings. The presence of minerals other than talc and the level of metamorphism can influence its hardness.
